blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A feature-flag client caches each flag for two minutes. On a cache hit it stores the current time in the flag's entry. The `new-checkout` flag is read by the checkout requests, about 40 a second. Operations switch it off at 10:00. When do checkout requests first see it off?

options.text: By 10:02, since the two minutes run from the load and the time each hit stores is kept only for statistics
options.says: the stored time is what the two minutes are measured from, and each hit overwrites it

options.text: Not while 40 reads a second keep arriving, since the two minutes restart from the time each hit stores
options.says: a flag read more often than every two minutes is never reloaded

options.text: By 10:02, since the two minutes run from the load, and the time each hit stores leaves the load time as it was
options.says: the entry keeps one time and each hit overwrites it, so the two minutes count from the last read

options.text: Not while 40 reads a second keep arriving, since the two minutes are checked only when no request is reading the flag
options.says: the age is checked on every read; the flag stays because each hit moves its stored time forward, so it never reaches two minutes

origin.section: Expiry Counted From the Last Read Keeps a Popular Price Forever

questions.stem: Shipping costs must use carrier tariffs at most one day old. A singleton service keeps `Map<String, Tariff> tariffs = new HashMap<>()` and returns `tariffs.computeIfAbsent(carrier, api::fetchTariff)`. It was last redeployed on a Friday. A carrier changes its tariff the next Monday. Which tariff does a shipment for that carrier use on Wednesday?

options.text: The new one, since a value stored for a day goes stale and is then fetched again
options.says: computeIfAbsent calls the function only when the key is absent or mapped to null; the value's age plays no part

options.text: The one fetched first after Friday's deploy, until the map grows large enough to be rebuilt
options.says: a resize keeps every entry and fetches nothing, so the first tariff stays

options.text: The one fetched first after Friday's deploy, since a key that is present is not fetched again
options.says: computeIfAbsent calls the function only for an absent key, and nothing removes the key, so the first tariff stays until the next restart

options.text: The new one, since each call fetches the tariff and the newer value replaces the stored one
options.says: the function runs once per key; later calls return the stored value without fetching

origin.section: Code Simpler Than the Requirement Is a Bug, Not KISS

questions.stem: A session registry is a `new LinkedHashMap<>(64, 0.75f, true)` whose `removeEldestEntry` keeps at most 5,000 sessions; the service never has more than 300. A support endpoint loops over `sessions.keySet()` and calls `sessions.get(id)` for each id to print it. What does the endpoint do in production, with 120 sessions and no other request running?

options.text: It prints all 120, since get rehashes the table once it holds more than 48 entries, and a rehash keeps the iteration order
options.says: get never rehashes; in an access-ordered map it moves the entry it reads to the end of the order, and the fail-fast iterator detects that

options.text: It prints all 120, since get moves each entry it reads to the end of the order, and a keySet iterator ignores changes of order
options.says: the javadoc counts that move as a structural modification, which the fail-fast iterator detects

options.text: It throws ConcurrentModificationException, since get rehashes the table once it holds more than 48 entries, which the keySet iterator detects
options.says: get never rehashes; in an access-ordered map it moves the one entry it reads to the end of the order, and that is what the iterator detects

options.text: It throws ConcurrentModificationException, since get moves each entry it reads to the end of the order, which the keySet iterator detects
options.says: the get reorders the map under its own iterator, and the next step of the fail-fast iterator throws

origin.section: An Option Nobody Needed Changes What Other Code May Do

questions.stem: Refund requests are validated by a rule map, `Map.of("amount", ..., "reason", ...)`, which an engine applies by calling `getClass().getMethod(key)` on the request record and invoking the result. A developer renames the record component `reason` to `refundReason` with the IDE's rename refactoring at its default settings. What happens next?

options.text: The build fails at the rule map, since javac matches each key against the record's accessor names
options.says: the keys are strings, and javac checks no strings

options.text: The build passes, and refund requests are rejected, since getMethod returns null for the missing name and the rule fails on null
options.says: getMethod throws NoSuchMethodException for a missing method; it never returns null

options.text: The build fails at the rename, since the IDE refuses to rename an accessor whose old name the rule map still holds
options.says: the rename updates Java references to the accessor, and a string literal is not one; nothing fails at build time

options.text: The build passes, and refund requests fail with an exception, since getMethod throws for the missing name
options.says: getMethod("reason") throws NoSuchMethodException when the first request is validated

origin.section: A Rule Engine for One Form Adds Failures the Plain Method Cannot Have

concepts: In an access-ordered LinkedHashMap, get moves the entry and is a structural modification, so a loop that calls get while iterating the keys throws ConcurrentModificationException once there are two entries.
computeIfAbsent calls its function only for an absent key, so a value it stored stays until the map is discarded.

Rules keyed by accessor names and applied by reflection are invisible to javac: a renamed component compiles and the engine fails at the first call, where a plain method call is renamed by the IDE or fails the build.
A general-purpose class brings rules the requirement never asked for, such as renewing entries on read, and each of them runs whether it is wanted or not.
